name: Aminata Diallo
headline: 19, apprentice plasterer, Dakar
description: Aminata Diallo wakes at 4:30 each morning, before the first call to prayer echoes through the dusty streets, and boils a large pot of millet porridge over a kerosene stove in the cramped room she rents with two other apprentices. She stirs with a long wooden paddle, her wrist moving in a steady, practiced rhythm, then pours the thick mixture into a battered metal pot and hoists it onto her head. She walks ten minutes to the construction site, where the workers are already stretching scaffolding and mixing cement. She sets up her small table near the gate, beside the heavy trucks, and sells her porridge in plastic bowls, scooping precisely measured amounts, wiping the ladle after each serving. She counts coins carefully, dropping each one into a cloth pouch she keeps tied to her waist, and she checks the pouch periodically, pressing it to feel the weight. She never gives credit, not even to foremen, and she smiles politely while shaking her head no—she learned that kindness in business leads to loss, and loss means she cannot pay for her school fees or send the small amount she saves for her younger sister's school supplies back home in the village where her mother and father still farm peanuts and millet, a place she left two years ago after the harvest failed and the eldest uncle said she must go to the city to earn something for the family, though he meant marriage, not training, but she convinced her mother to let her learn a trade that would make her independent, a trade her mother had once seen a woman do on a visit to the next town, smoothing cement walls with a trowel, a sight that made Aminata whisper to her mother that she could do that too, and now she does it, six days a week, in the government-run trade school that sits behind a high concrete wall with a metal gate that clangs shut at seven in the evening. In the afternoons, after the porridge pot is empty and the construction workers have returned to their hammers, she walks to the school, her feet carrying her past open gutters and the smell of diesel, and she enters the plastering workshop, a long room with half-finished walls of brick and sand, each assigned to a student. There, she scoops plaster from a mixing trough, adds water from a bucket, and stirs with a trowel, testing the consistency with her index finger, feeling for the right smoothness. She spreads the plaster onto the wall in long, even strokes, her elbow moving like a lever, her shoulder tight, and then she steps back, tilts her head, looks at the surface under the harsh fluorescent light, and pulls out her small, scratched cellphone—a model she bought secondhand from a street vendor—and takes a careful photo of the wall, making sure the angle captures the light hitting the trowel marks. She keeps the photos in a folder labeled 'walls,' and every evening, after she returns to the rented room and eats a simple dinner of rice and beans with her two roommates—Serge, who is learning plumbing, and Mariam, who is learning tiling—she sits on her thin mattress and scrolls through the photos, comparing them, noting where the strokes are too thick, where the corners are soft, where the surface dips, and she makes mental notes, sometimes even sketching in a small notebook with a stubby pencil, drawing arrows and circles around the problem areas. Her roommates tease her about the photos, saying she is obsessed, but she just nods and says she needs to see where she fumbled. She is cautious with her words, speaking in short, measured sentences, and she watches others before she acts, studying the way the instructor moves his wrist, the way Serge bends his back when he works, the way Mariam taps a tile to check for hollow sounds—she stores all of that in her head, methodical, patient, always learning. She keeps her wages in a tin box hidden inside a hole in the floor beneath her mattress, packed in a plastic bag to keep out moisture, and she counts it each Sunday morning, writing the total on a scrap of paper that she burns afterward in the charcoal stove. She does not trust banks. She watched a bank in the town of her birth collapse when she was twelve, and the owners fled with the money, and her neighbor lost everything she had saved for her funeral. Aminata learned then that paper promises can burn like ash, and she prefers the weight of coins and crumpled notes under her own palm, where she can see them, touch them, know they are real. She is also cautious about people, but not unkind; she shares her porridge occasionally with a stray dog, and she helps Mariam carry heavy bags of tile, but she never tells anyone exactly how much she saves, and she never talks about her family, because she knows that words carry seeds, and she would rather plant them only where she can tend them. At night, before she sleeps, she runs her thumb over the screen of her cellphone, looking at the photo of the last wall she plastered—smooth in places, rough in others—and she plans what she will do differently tomorrow morning when she practices before class, even though she will wake exhausted, because she is building something more than walls: she is building a person who can shape her own life, stroke by stroke.
